overview.body:
**Hoori** ​(*hoori*) — ‌Agriculture, ‌Hunter ​· Fire-subduing ​— ​belongs to ​the ​Japanese ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Agriculture, ​Hunter". ‌The name ​means ​"Fire-subduing"[^1].

**Hoori** ​is ​the ​younger son ‌of ​Ninigi and ‌Konohana-Sakuya-hime, ​the ‌husband of ​the ‌sea princess ​Toyotama, ‌and ​the great-grandfather ​of ‌Japan's first ‌emperor, ‌Jimmu. His ​name, ​'Fire-Subduing,' ‌marks him ​as ​the brother ‌who ​overcame ​Hoderi's fire ‌and ​whose line ‌would ​rule ​the land.[^2]

​PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ‌as ​**Hoori** and ‌serves ​its temple ​at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/hoori/). ‌The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII ‌form *hoori* ​survives ​as a ​modern ‌convenience ​imposed by ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system; ​the restoration, ‌not ‌the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ​project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**火折命**. ​Etymologically ‌it ​means ​"Fire-subduing"[^1].

‌The ​ASCII ‌form ​*hoori* survives ‌only ​because ​the ​early ​domain-name ​system ‌could ​not ‌carry diacritics; ​it ‌is ​a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ​ancient ‌spelling. ‌The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Hoori** ​recovers ‌the ​full ​diacritic ‌detail ​of ​the ‌scholarly transliteration ​directly ‌in ​the ​address ​bar. ​The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— a ​description ​computed ‌from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form ​itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**h** ‌→ ​**H** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**o** ​→ ​**o** — ‌Same
- ​**o** ‌→ ​**o** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**r** ‌→ ​**r** ​— Same
- ​**i** ​→ ‌**i** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Kojiki I (Hoori–Hoderi cycle; Aston, tr. I; Philippi, tr.).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is **/hoː.ɾi/** ​— ​Modern Standard ​Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**Hō-** ​— Voiceless ‌glottal ​[h] plus ‌long ​open-mid back ‌[oː]; from ​火 ​'fire'
- **-ri** ​— ​Alveolar tap ​[ɾ] ‌plus close ​front [i]; ‌from ​折 'to ‌subdue/break'

​For the ‌modern speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: ​'HOH-ree' — ‌hold ‌the first ‌syllable long; ​the ​'r' is ‌a ​light tap.

​Kindred ‌and historical ​forms of ​the ‌name:

- **Japanese** ​— ‌火折命 (Hoori-no-mikoto), ​'Fire-Subduing Lord' ​(Kojiki); ​also 彦火火出見尊 ​Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto
- ‌**Brother** — ‌Hoderi ​(火照命, Fire-Shining ‌Lord), his ​elder ​brother, master ‌of ‌the sea's ‌fortune
- ‌**Descendant** — ​Great-grandfather of ‌Emperor ​Jimmu through ​his ​son Ugayafukiaezu ‌(Kojiki I; ​Nihon ​Shoki I)

​Hoori ‌is a ​plain ​restoration in ​this restoration: ‌the ​long ō ‌is ​not represented, ‌so ​the ASCII ‌form is ‌identical ​to Hepburn. ​He ​is a ​pivotal ancestor ‌in ‌the imperial ​genealogy.

sources.citation: Kojiki I (Hoori–Hoderi cycle; Aston, tr. I; Philippi, tr.).

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**火折命**. ​This ‌original script ​is ​the ‌form ​against ‌which ​the ‌ASCII fallback ​*hoori* ​and ​the ​PuniCodex ​restoration ‌**Hoori** are ​measured: ‌the ​restoration ‌preserves ​its ‌full diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the ​written ‌form, ‌so ‌that a ​reader ​typing ‌the ​modern ​address ‌still speaks ​the ​ancient ‌name.[^1]

​The ‌Kojiki ​writes his ​name ​火折命, ​Hoori-no-mikoto, ‌conventionally ‌glossed ​'Fire-Subduing Lord': ‌火 ​'fire' ​+ ‌折 ‌'to ‌break, ‌subdue' + ​命, ‌the ​honorific ​for ​a ‌kami. The ​same ​prince ​bears ‌the ​fuller ​name 彦火火出見尊, ​Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto. ‌His ​brother ‌is ​火照命 ‌Hoderi-no-mikoto, ​'Fire-Shining Lord' ‌— ‌one ​word ​burns ​steady, ​the other ‌breaks ‌what ​burns.

sources.citation: Kojiki I (Hoori–Hoderi cycle; Aston, tr. I; Philippi, tr.).

domains.body:
**Hoori** ​is ‌the ‌younger son ​of ​Ninigi ​and ​Konohana-Sakuya-hime, ​the ‌husband ​of the ​sea ‌princess ​Toyotama, ‌and ​the ‌great-grandfather ​of Japan's ​first ​emperor, ​Jimmu. ​His ‌name, ​'Fire-Subduing,' ‌marks him ​as ‌the ​brother ‌who ​overcame ‌Hoderi's fire ​and ​whose ‌line ‌would ‌rule ​the ​land.[^1]

### Master ‌of ​the ​Mountains

‌He ​received ​the ‌bow and ​became ‌a ​hunter ​of ​the ​highlands.

### ‌Husband of ‌Toyotama

​Married ‌the ​daughter ​of ‌the ‌sea god ‌Ryūjin ‌in ​the ‌undersea ​palace.

### ​Father of ​Ugayafukiaezu

‌His ​son ​by ​Toyotama ‌continued ​the line ​to ​Emperor ‌Jimmu.

### ​Imperial ‌Forebear

​His ‌story explains ​how ‌the ‌imperial ​line ​gained ​legitimacy ​from both ‌sea ‌and ​land.

Kojiki I (Hoori–Hoderi cycle; Aston, tr. I; Philippi, tr.).

mythology.body:
Hoori's mythology is the bridge ​between the heavenly descent of Ninigi and the ‌earthly reign of Emperor Jimmu: a story of ‌exchanged tools, a lost hook, a voyage to the ​dragon palace, a broken promise, and a line ​of kings. It is told in the Kojiki ​and repeated, with variations, in the Nihon Shoki.[^1]

### ​The Exchanged Tools (Kojiki)

The youngest son of Ninigi ​and Konohana-Sakuya-hime received from his father the **bow**, ‌while his elder brother Hoderi received the **fishhook** ​— one son of the mountains, one of the ​sea, mirroring the division of the land itself ‌(Kojiki I). Hoori proposed that they exchange tools ​for a single day: he would try his ‌brother's fortune with the hook, Hoderi the mountains with ​the bow. The day went well for no ‌one. Hoori, inexpert at the shore, lost the ​borrowed hook in the sea, and when he dived ​and dragged the bottom it could not be ​found. Hoderi refused every substitute — first his ​own sword, then five hundred mother-of-pearl hooks, then a ​thousand — demanding back the one original hook, ‌the single object through which a man's fortune ​was thought to run. The impossible demand drives ‌the younger brother out of the human world and ​down into the sea: the quarrel over one ‌small thing is what opens the door to ​the gods.[^2]

### The Dragon Palace of Watasumi (Kojiki)

Following ‌the counsel of an old man on the ​beach — one of the passing kami who ‌advise heroes at their lowest hour — Hoori sat ​on the bough of a tree that bent ​over the waves until the tide carried him ‌down through a gateway into the undersea palace ‌of **Watasumi-no-kami**, the sea deity. There he was welcomed, ‌bathed, feasted, and married to the sea god's ​daughter **Toyotama-hime**, the 'Abundant-Jewel Princess' (Kojiki I). When ​Hoori confessed why he had come, Toyotama's brother searched ‌the sea and recovered the lost hook from ​the throat of a red sea-bream. Watasumi then ​gave his son-in-law two treasures — the tide-flowing ‌jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel, with which any sea ​can be raised or stilled — and taught ​him the ruse by which a proud man ‌is broken: do not answer rage with rage, but ​**mock it gently as it rages**, and its ‌strength will spend itself against your calm. The ​palace gives the exiled brother everything his own shore ​withheld: a wife, the hook, and a strategy.

### ​The Mocked Brother and the Covenant (Kojiki)

Hoori ​returned to land and waited on the beach. ‌When Hoderi came raging across the strand, Hoori sang ‌a mocking song — as the Kojiki has ​it, like the bushes on the shore his ‌brother's beard was tangled, like the drifting seaweed his ​rage floated aimlessly — and Hoderi attacked. Hoori ​raised the tide-flowing jewel, and the sea rose ‌to Hoderi's neck; Hoderi begged and wept, and ‌Hoori raised the ebbing jewel and spared him (Kojiki ‌I). The brothers made peace on a new ‌order: Hoderi would keep the watery ways, and ​his descendants would serve Hoori's line forever. Thus the ‌sea-fortune and the mountain-fortune were divided as they ​still are in Japan — and the humbler ​brother, who had lost everything in the water, came ​home owning both the land and the sea's ‌obedience. The myth's arithmetic is deliberate: the borrowed ​hook cost nothing to replace, but the brotherly ​covenant it purchased was the real prize.

### The Broken ​Taboo and the First Emperor (Kojiki)

Toyotama came ‌up from the sea to bear her child, ​but first she built a parturition hut roofed with ​cormorant feathers and laid down the law that ​Hoori must not look inside. Curiosity — the ‌flaw and the engine of this whole cycle — ​overcame him. He peeked and saw his wife ‌in her true shape, a great **sea-dragon** coiled ​in the hut; mortified, Toyotama abandoned the land ‌and the newborn, sending her sister **Tamayori-hime** in her ​place with a parting song. The child, **Ugayafukiaezu**, ‌was raised by his aunt, married her in ‌time, and their son was Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko — better known ​as **Emperor Jimmu**, first emperor of Japan (Kojiki ​I; Nihon Shoki I). Hoori's one act of ​disobedience costs him his wife, yet it leaves ​the imperial line on land, guarded by sea and ‌mountain at once. The sources read the episode ‌without apology: the line of emperors begins exactly ​where the promise was broken.

syncretism.body:
Hoori's ​story fuses ‌motifs common ‌across East ​Asia: the ​mortal who ​journeys to ​the dragon ​palace (parallels ‌in Chinese ​and Korean ​legend), the ‌animal bride ​whose true ‌form must ​never be ‌seen, and ​the younger ​brother whose ​misfortune ripens ​into sovereignty. ​Within Japan ‌the dragon-palace ​voyage lived ‌on most ​famously in ‌the folktale ​of **Urashima ‌Tarō**, where ​the same ‌palace, the ​same time-slip, ​and the ‌same broken ‌promise end ‌far more ​cruelly. Buddhist ​Japan had ‌no need ​to give ​Hoori an ‌avatar — ​his tale ​was too ‌useful ​to the ‌state to ​remain folklore. ​Written into ​the Kojiki ​(712) and ‌Nihon Shoki ‌(720), it ​became the ‌founding charter ​of the ​imperial house, ‌read at ‌court and ‌cited by ‌every dynasty ​that traced ‌itself to ​Jimmu. The ​motifs are ​pan-Asian; the ‌genealogy is ​specifically Yamato.[^1]

​Kindred figures ​in the ‌PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include ​[[hoderi|Hoderi]] (elder ​and younger ‌fire brothers), ​[[toyotama|Toyotama]] (hunter ‌husband and ​sea wife), ‌[[ugayafukiaezu|Ugayafukiaezu]] (father ​and ancestor ‌of Jimmu), ‌[[anahita|Anāhitā]] (earth ​/ mother ​/ fertility), ​[[anat|ꜥAnat]] (hunt ​/ wild), ‌and [[artemis|Ártemis]] ‌(hunt / ​wild).

sources.citation: Kojiki I (Hoori–Hoderi cycle; Aston, tr. I; Philippi, tr.).

cultural-legacy.body: Hoori ​is ‌remembered almost ‌entirely ​as ​an ​ancestor, but ​his ​story ‌has ​never stopped ​being ‌retold. ​The dragon ‌palace ​resurfaces ‌in ​Heian tales, ​in ​*otogizōshi* ​storybooks, ​in puppet-theatre ‌and ​Kabuki ‌adaptations, ​and in ‌modern ​novels, ‌manga, ​and anime ‌— ​the ​sea-bride ‌and the ‌undersea ‌court ​are among ​Japan's ‌most ​durable ​images. Politically ‌his ​line ​still ‌matters: the ​traditional ‌date ​of ​Jimmu's accession, ​the ​first ‌day ‌of the ​first ‌month ​of 660 ​BCE, ‌became ‌*Kigensetsu* ‌in 1872 ‌and ​survives ‌as ​National Foundation ​Day ​(11 ‌February). ​The imperial ​regalia ​— ‌mirror, ​sword, and ​jewel ​— ‌descend ​through this ‌very ​genealogy, ‌so that ​Hoori's ‌tide-jewels ‌and ​his descendants' ​legitimacy ​remain, ​ritually, ‌in the ‌same ​family.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki I (Hoori–Hoderi cycle; Aston, tr. I; Philippi, tr.).

archaeology.body: Hoori ​has no ‌shrine ‌and no ​image, ​but ​his story ​is ​anchored in ‌real ​ground. The ​Kojiki ‌and Nihon ​Shoki ‌place the ​action ‌in ​the Yamato ​basin: ​Jimmu's traditional ​tomb, ​the Unebi ‌kofun, ​lies by ‌Kashihara ​in Nara ‌Prefecture, ​and ‌**Kashihara Jingū** ​— ‌founded in ​1890 ​— marks ‌the ‌traditional site ‌of ​Kashihara-no-miya, the ​palace ‌from ​which Jimmu ​set ‌out eastward. ​His ​narrative survives ‌materially ​in the ‌**Shinpukuji-bon**, ​the early ​thirteenth-century ​manuscript ​of the ‌Kojiki ‌kept at ​Shinpuku-ji ‌in Nagoya, ​the ​sole complete ‌copy ‌of the ‌lost ‌712 ​original. At ‌the ​foot of ​Mount ​Miwa, the ‌Ōmiwa ​shrine preserves ​the ​sacred landscape ‌in ​which ​the Jimmu-cycle ​myths ‌were first ​localized. ‌The evidence ​is ‌commemorative rather ​than ‌contemporary — ‌but ​for ​an eighth-century ​state ​charter, that ‌is ‌precisely the ​point.[^1]

meditation.body: Hoori ​is the ‌one who ‌looked. His ​whole ​career turns ​on small ​acts ​with enormous ‌consequences: he ​borrows a ​hook ‌and loses ​an empire's ‌worth of ​trouble; ‌he accepts ​a bride ​and ​gains the ​sea; he ​peeks through ‌a ​feathered wall ‌and loses ​her — ‌and ​founds a ‌dynasty. The ​Kojiki ‌does not ​condemn him. ​Instead it ‌makes ‌curiosity the ‌very mechanism ​by which ​the ‌imperial line ​comes to ​land: ‌no broken ​taboo, no ​Jimmu. It ‌is ​a strikingly ‌unsentimental theology ​of legitimacy, ​closer ​to a ​political founding ‌document ‌than a ​moral tale: ‌the state ​begins ​not in ‌obedience but ‌in transgression ‌survived. ‌Hoori also ​teaches a ‌subtler ​lesson about ​rivalry. He ​never defeats ‌his ​brother by ​force; he ​wins by ‌patience, ​by the ​tide-jewels, and ​by ‌a mocking ​song. The ‌victor in ​this ‌myth is ​the one ‌who can ‌wait ​on the ​beach while ​his ​brother's rage ‌exhausts itself ‌against the ​sea.[^1]
